title: Trump Visits Army War College to Talk About Big Military Tech—But There’s a Missile Shortage
summary: Have you ever run out of your favorite snack and the store won’t have more for weeks? That’s kind of what’s happening with some of America’s most important weapons. On Wednesday, President Donald Trump visited the U.S. Army War College in Carlisle, Pennsylvania, to talk about investing in cool new battlefield technology. The event was organized by Senator David McCormick, and lots of big names were there—like the CEOs of Lockheed Martin, Boeing, and SpaceX. But behind the exciting talk, there’s a problem. Because of the war in Iran, the U.S. has been firing off lots of Tomahawk cruise missiles and Patriot and THAAD interceptors (those are missiles that knock down enemy missiles). Now, stockpiles are low. An analysis in May said it could take at least three years to make enough new ones. That’s a long time, especially with worries about possible future conflicts, like with China. Trump wants a huge $1.5 trillion defense budget for next year to fix this, but Congress hasn’t approved it yet. Even if they do, building more missiles takes time. The summit also talked about new investments—like $10 million for AI research and a new 10,000-square-foot robotics factory in Pittsburgh. But for now, the military is like a kid with an empty snack drawer, waiting for the delivery truck.
why_it_matters: Just like running out of your favorite snack can be a problem, having too few important weapons can leave a country less safe, and fixing it takes careful planning and a long time.

background_read: The U.S. uses missiles like Tomahawks (long-range weapons fired from ships) to strike faraway targets, and Patriot and THAAD interceptors to shoot down enemy missiles.
Stockpiles are the supplies of weapons a country keeps ready. When they get low, rebuilding them takes years because the missiles are very complex to manufacture.
Congress (the group of lawmakers in Washington, D.C.) is the one that decides how much money the military can spend each year.

perspectives.description: They believe a huge defense budget and new technology will make America stronger and more secure against threats.
They warn that low missile supplies mean the country might not be ready if a big conflict starts soon, and rebuilding those supplies takes many years.
They worry that spending so much money on the military could mean less money for other important things like schools or healthcare.
